# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–27 (Complete – Updated 192)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn in continental Europe, seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; **Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; Pumpernickel (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen**.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness. Old Sedley forgave past grievances, confessing unkindness to Amelia. Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
Osborne's mind visibly changing in final months. Asked Georgy about Jos; invited Jos and Dobbin to dinner where every family plate was exhibited. Osborne asked Dobbin repeatedly about Mrs. George Osborne. Dobbin spoke eloquently of Amelia's sufferings, passionate attachment to husband's memory, tender duty to parents, sacrifice of boy. Osborne replied: "By God, you are a good feller, sir." Reconciliation meeting never took place. Old Sedley's lingering illness intervened. Osborne found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Pocket of dressing-gown contained letter from George written from Waterloo and key to box of son's papers; seals broken—likely read night before seizure while reading great red family Bible in study. Died in four days without speaking again.

**Will Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house affairs. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds, chargeable on George's property, left to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who was to resume guardianship of boy. Major William Dobbin appointed executor, named "my beloved son's friend." Will stated Osborne maintained grandson and widow "when they were otherwise without means of support" and bequeathed sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit." Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation and New Life (Chapter 26)
Upon learning of William's bounty supporting her in poverty, Amelia "sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart." Visited deserted Gaunt House in deep sables. Found straw littered in front, great blank rooms bearing marks where pictures and mirrors hung. At George's upper room window (where she once gazed as child), looked out over Russell Square toward her birthplace. Thought of "man who had been her constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend." Took temporary house at Richmond. During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character—generous aims, constant truth, elevated degree, lack of meanness making him simple, honest face, warm and humble heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour Details (Chapter 26)
Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne. Jos announced arrival in Cologne newspapers as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London." Had court dress; insisted Dobbin bring regimental paraphernalia; announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Left own card and Major's on "Our Minister" wherever party stopped. Kept journal noting defects or excellences of inns and wines. Slept good deal after dinner or basked in arbours. Observed Earl of Bareacres and family on ship; both "looked rather younger" than remembered from Brussels in '15, with Lady's dark hair now "a beautiful golden auburn" and Lord's red whiskers now "of a rich black with purple and green reflections." Amelia very happy and pleased. Dobbin carried her stool and sketch-book, admired her drawings. She sat upon steamers' decks and drew crags and castles, or mounted upon donkeys to ascend ancient robber-towers, attended by Georgy and Dobbin. She laughed at Major's droll figure on donkey-back with long legs touching ground. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26–27)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre in Pumpernickel. Upon "burst of that beloved and well-known music," every Englishman in house proclaimed membership in British nation—"Sir John and Lady Bullminster (who had taken a house at Pumpernickel for the education of their nine children), the fat gentleman with the mustachios, the long Major in white duck trousers, and the lady with the little boy." Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased), rose in his box and bowed.

**Tapeworm's Attentions**: Near end of performance, Tapeworm approached Jos with "fascinating smile" and invitation to stay in Pumpernickel. "My lord nearly sent Jos off his legs...with a Parthian grin and glance which he thought must finish Mrs. Osborne completely."

**Lodging and Social Advancement**: Tapeworm accepted Jos's invitation to lodge at his quarters. Put dexterous questions to Jos about India and dancing-girls; asked Amelia about "that beautiful boy" (Georgy); complimented her upon "prodigious sensation which she had made in the house"; tried to fascinate Dobbin talking of late war and Pumpernickel contingent exploits. Doctor von Glauber speedily convinced Jos that Pumpernickel mineral springs and Doctor's particular treatment would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Jos's mind made up; committed to spend autumn in Pumpernickel. Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII, conducted by Count de Schlusselback, Marshal of the Court. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression."

**Emmy at Court and Evening Dress**: Emmy presented to august family. On certain days mourning not admitted at Court, so she appeared in pink crape dress with diamond ornament in corsage presented by her brother. "She looked so pretty in this costume that the Duke and Court (putting out of the question the Major, who had scarcely ever seen her before in an evening dress, and vowed that she did not look five-and-twenty) all admired her excessively."

**Pumpernickel Government and Society**: Constitution moderate despotism tempered by Chamber that might or might not be elected. Prime Minister lodged in second floor; Foreign Secretary occupied comfortable lodgings over Zwieback's Conditorey. Army consisted of magnificent band that also did duty on stage. Noble society divided into factions: Strumpff faction (supported by Tapeworm, English) and Lederlung party (supported by French Charge d'Affaires M. de Macabau). Politics ran very high; parties very bitter. Strumpff was greater singer, stout, not in first youth and beauty; Lederlung pretty creature with sweet voice. Two women were "two flags of the French and the English party at Pumpernickel." Society divided in allegiance to those two great nations. French party included Foreign Minister, Commander-in-Chief's Lady (who served under Napoleon), Hof-Marschall and his wife. English party included Home Minister, Master of the Horse, Duke's Private Secretary, Prince's Tutor. Secretary of French Chancery was little Grignac, young fellow, malicious, made caricatures of Tapeworm in albums of place.

**Theatre and Court Entertainment**: Theatre of Pumpernickel known and famous in that quarter of Germany. Present Duke in youth insisted upon having his own operas played there; one day in fury from orchestra place broke bassoon on Chapel Master's head, leading too slow. Duchess Sophia wrote domestic comedies. Prince executes music in private now; Duchess gives away her plays to foreigners of distinction. Court conducted with comfort and splendour. When balls held with four hundred people at supper, servant in scarlet and lace attended upon every four; all served on silver. Festivals and entertainments going continually on. Gardens arranged to emulate those of Versailles; allegorical waterworks include Trophonius' cave with leaden Tritons spouting water and playing groans from lead conchs, nymphbath, Niagara cataract, admired at yearly fair at Chamber opening and fetes celebrating princely governors' birthdays and marriage-days.

**Emmy's Social Activities (Chapter 27)**: Before winter far advanced, Emmy took night and received company with great propriety and modesty. Had French master who complimented her upon purity of accent and facility of learning; she had learned long ago and grounded herself subsequently in grammar to teach George. Madam Strumpff came to give her lessons in singing, performed so well with such true voice that Major's windows opposite (lodgings under Prime Minister) were always open to hear lesson. German ladies, very sentimental and simple, fell in love with her and called her du at once. Major made himself George's tutor, read Caesar and mathematics with him; they had German master and rode out of evenings by side of Emmy's carriage. Emmy too timid, made dreadful outcry at slightest disturbance on horse-back. Drove about with one of dear German friends, Jos asleep on back-seat of barouche.

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26–27)
Now eleven years old; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. On continental tour: walked ahead during excursions, climbing towers and trees, while Amelia and Dobbin walked soberly below. Made "prodigious advance in the knowledge of High Dutch" conversing with Herr Kirsch on carriage box. Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Will restored him to mother's guardianship. Boy remained active, imperious, good-natured.

## Jos's Romantic Interest (Chapter 27)
**Plan with Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod**: Jos becoming very sweet upon Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod, very gentle tender-hearted and unassuming young creature, a Canoness and Countess in her own right but with scarcely ten pounds per year to her fortune. Fanny declared that to be Amelia's sister was greatest delight Heaven could bestow. Jos might have put Countess's shield and coronet by side of own arms on carriage and forks. **Interrupted by Events**: When grand fetes given upon marriage of Hereditary Prince of Pumpernickel with lovely Princess Amelia of Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen took place, events occurred.

## Reconciliation with Mrs. Frederick Bullock (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock, "although despoiled by that little monster of one-half of the sum which she expected from her father, nevertheless showed her charitableness of spirit by being reconciled to the mother and the boy." One day chariot with golden bullocks emblazoned on panels drove to Amelia's house. Bullock family made irruption into garden where Amelia was reading, Jos in arbour dipping strawberries into wine, Major in Indian jacket giving back to Georgy for jumping over him. Those ladies met "after an absence of more than fifteen years." Per Rowdy and Hollyock's conversation, Mrs. Bullock "is always scheming and managing. She wants Mrs. Osborne's account to be taken from our house to hers--and the way in which she coaxes that boy and makes him sit by that blear-eyed little Rosa is perfectly ridiculous."

## Miss Swartz's Renewed Friendship (Chapter 26)
Old friend Miss Swartz and husband came thundering over from Hampton Court with flaming yellow liveries, "as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever."

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne.

## Rebecca's Fate (Chapter 24)
Bailiffs seized Curzon Street property. Rawdon made her "tolerable annuity." Whereabouts unknown; "Who cared!"
